<reason>Both sides debated at a high level, and B's meta-argument ("you keep defending a different policy") was the sharpest line of the exchange. But A wins on the decisive clash: the motion as written already keys fees to size-imposed costs ("when their size imposes higher safety and street-use costs"), and B conceded in B4.5 that cost-keyed pricing is acceptable in principle — reducing B's case to a drafting quibble about the word "oversized." A also neutralized B's exposure objection by noting that two of the motion's three instruments (parking and curb fees) charge per hour and per foot at every use, continuous exposure pricing comparable to the fuel tax B praised, and A's measurement dilemma (kills congestion pricing and fuel taxes if applied consistently) was only partially escaped. B's funding alternative (general revenue, fines, meters) was coherent but conceded that safety spending needs revenue the fee provides. A answered both pressure questions directly and crisply; B answered both as well, but B's answers leaned on the "different policy" reframe rather than defeating A's interpretation of the motion text. A's closing more cleanly crystallized the weighing of alternatives (federal authority, revenue, timing) that had accumulated over the round.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The B4.5/A5.1 exchange: B landed "every time PRO defends this policy, they describe a different one," which was the most dangerous moment for A — but A's reply that the motion's conditional clause ("when size imposes higher costs") plus the word "oversized" already embeds the cost-keying, combined with B's own concession that a measured-cost fee is acceptable, converted B's strongest weapon into a label dispute rather than a principled objection.</best_rebuttal>
